lessons.title: Acid Etching and Frosting
lessons.body: Acid etching uses hydrofluoric acid (HF) or ammonium bifluoride to create a frosted, matte finish on glass. In Africa, small workshops often use a paste made from ammonium bifluoride (ABF) and a thickener like cornstarch or bentonite clay. A typical mix: 100g ABF powder, 50g cornstarch, and 200ml water. Stir into a paste. Apply with a brush or roller to clean glass. Leave for 3-10 minutes depending on desired depth. Rinse thoroughly with plenty of water. Neutralize with baking soda solution. Always wear nitrile gloves, goggles, and a respirator with acid gas cartridges. Work outdoors or with strong ventilation. HF is extremely dangerousâit penetrates skin and attacks bones. Never use HF without proper training. ABF is safer but still corrosive. For frosting, you can also use a cream from suppliers like Bohle or local chemical companies in South Africa, Kenya, or Nigeria. Cost: about $20-$50 per liter of ready-to-use cream. A liter covers 2-3 square meters. For deeper etch, use 48% HF but only in professional setups. After etching, clean with water and dry with a squeegee. You can create patterns using vinyl stencils or masking tape. Cut design, stick to glass, apply paste, wait, rinse. Remove stencil. For a gradient effect, vary dwell time. Safety: keep a calcium gluconate gel on hand for HF burnsâit's a medical emergency. In many African countries, ABF is available from pottery suppliers or online. Store in plastic containers, never metal. Dispose of waste by neutralizing with lime or soda ash. This technique is used for decorative panels, privacy windows, and shower doors. It's a low-cost way to add value to plain glass.

lessons.title: Sandblasting and Abrasive Etching
lessons.body: Sandblasting (abrasive blasting) uses compressed air to propel fine abrasive particles against glass, creating a frosted or carved surface. In Africa, many workshops use a simple siphon-feed blaster or a pressure pot. You need a compressor delivering at least 90 PSI and 10 CFM. Abrasives: aluminum oxide (80-120 grit) or silicon carbide. Don't use silica sandâit causes silicosis. For a small setup, a cabinet blaster costs $500-$1500. For large panels, a portable pressure blaster with a hand-held nozzle works. First, clean glass. Apply a resist: rubber masking film, vinyl, or thick tape. Cut your design with a knife. For deep carving, use a hard resist like 3M sandblast stencil. Blast at 60-90 PSI, holding nozzle 10-15 cm from surface. Move steadily. Frosting takes 10-20 seconds per area; deep carve takes minutes. Practice on scrap. For even frosting, use multiple passes. After blasting, remove resist. Clean with water and a soft brush. For a polished look, you can flame-polish or acid-polish the carved areas, but that's advanced. Safety: wear a NIOSH-approved respirator (P100), goggles, hearing protection, and gloves. Work in a blast cabinet or ventilated area. In Africa, abrasive suppliers exist in major citiesâcheck industrial hardware stores. Aluminum oxide costs about $2-$5 per kg. A 25kg bag lasts a while. You can also use a sandblasting gun with a small compressor for touch-ups. Common applications: frosted logos, privacy glass, decorative panels, and gravestones. For a two-tone effect, blast at different pressures or with different grits. Remember: always test on scrap glass first. Keep nozzle perpendicular for even etch. Clean nozzle regularly to avoid clogging.

lessons.title: Chemical Vapor Deposition (CVD) Coatings
lessons.body: Chemical Vapor Deposition (CVD) is an industrial process that deposits thin films on glass by reacting gases at high temperatures. In glass processing, CVD is used to make low-emissivity (low-E) coatings, which reflect heat back into a room. The most common CVD method for glass is online CVD, done during float glass production. Precursors like tin tetrachloride and silane are injected onto the hot glass surface (around 600Â°C) where they decompose and form a thin metal oxide layer. This layer is only 10-50 nanometers thick. For a small-scale African workshop, CVD is not practicalâit requires a furnace, gas handling, and safety systems costing millions. However, you can buy CVD-coated glass from major manufacturers like Saint-Gobain, Pilkington, or Chinese suppliers. If you want to apply a coating yourself, you'd use off-line methods like sputtering or sol-gel. But understanding CVD helps you identify glass types. CVD low-E glass is pyrolytic, meaning the coating is baked into the glass and can be tempered. It has a slight haze and is durable. You can cut, drill, and temper it. For building projects in Africa, specify CVD low-E for energy efficiency. It reduces cooling loads by up to 30%. Cost: $30-$80 per square meter. Installation: handle with care, but no special edge deletion needed. Clean with non-abrasive cleaners. If you're a fabricator, you can buy CVD-coated glass and process it like normal glass. Just avoid scratching the coating. For a small business, the opportunity is in selling and installing energy-efficient glass, not making it. You can partner with suppliers. Training: watch videos on how low-E glass is made to understand quality. Look for 'online CVD glass production' on YouTube. The key takeaway: CVD is a factory process, but you can profit from using its products.

lessons.title: Magnetron Sputtering for Low-E Coatings
lessons.body: Magnetron sputtering is a vacuum coating process used to make high-performance low-E glass. In a vacuum chamber, a metal target (like silver) is bombarded with ions, ejecting atoms that deposit onto glass. For low-E, a stack of layers is deposited: dielectric, silver, dielectric. The silver layer (10-15 nm) reflects infrared heat. Sputtering is done off-line in a large vacuum coater. For an African entrepreneur, buying a sputtering system is expensive ($1M+), but you can buy sputtered low-E glass from suppliers. Sputtered low-E is softer than CVD low-E and must be used in an insulated glass unit (IGU) with the coating on the inside. It cannot be tempered after coating. You must edge-delete the coating before making IGUs to ensure sealant adhesion. Edge deletion is done with a grinding wheel or sandblaster. For a small workshop, you can buy pre-coated glass and fabricate IGUs. Cost of sputtered low-E glass: $40-$100 per square meter. To identify: it has a slight color (blue or green) and high reflectivity. Handle with glovesâfingerprints damage the coating. Clean with a soft cloth and mild detergent. In Africa, demand for low-E glass is growing in upscale buildings. You can market energy savings: low-E glass reduces heat gain by 50-70%. For installation, ensure the coating faces the air gap. If you want to learn sputtering, visit a local glass factory or watch videos on 'magnetron sputtering glass coating'. There are also DIY sputtering systems for small-scale, but they are not for architectural glass. Focus on sourcing and installing quality low-E glass. Partner with a supplier who can provide technical data. Always check the emissivity (0.05-0.15 for low-E). This is a high-value skill for green building projects.

lessons.title: Sol-Gel Coatings
lessons.body: Sol-gel is a low-cost, wet-chemical method to apply thin coatings on glass. You mix a precursor like tetraethyl orthosilicate (TEOS) with water, alcohol, and acid catalyst. This forms a sol (liquid). You dip, spin, or spray it onto glass. Then it gels and dries, forming a porous silica layer. For African workshops, sol-gel is accessible: TEOS costs about $20 per liter. You can make anti-reflective (AR) coatings, self-cleaning (photocatalytic) coatings with titanium dioxide, or hydrophobic coatings. For AR coating: mix TEOS, ethanol, water, and HCl in molar ratio 1:10:4:0.01. Stir for 2 hours. Dip clean glass, withdraw at 10 cm/min. Dry at 100Â°C for 1 hour, then bake at 400Â°C for 1 hour if glass can withstand. This creates a porous layer with low refractive index, reducing reflection from 4% to 1%. For self-cleaning: use titanium isopropoxide, hydrolyze, dip, and bake at 500Â°C. The coating breaks down dirt with UV light. For hydrophobic: add a silane like trimethoxy(octadecyl)silane. Apply by dip or spray. Cure at 120Â°C. Sol-gel is great for small-scale production: you can coat mirrors, solar panels, or decorative glass. Safety: work in a fume hood, wear gloves and goggles. Chemicals are flammable. In Africa, source chemicals from lab suppliers or online. A simple dip coater can be made with a pulley and motor. Cost per square meter: $2-$10. The main challenge is durabilityâsol-gel coatings scratch easily unless baked. For outdoor use, add a protective topcoat. You can also use commercial sol-gel kits. Training: search 'sol-gel glass coating DIY' on YouTube. This is a skill that can set your workshop apart. Start with small pieces, test adhesion with tape test. If it passes, you're ready to offer custom coatings.

lessons.title: Anti-Reflective and Mirror Coatings
lessons.body: Anti-reflective (AR) coatings reduce glare and increase light transmission. They are essential for solar panels, display glass, and picture framing. In Africa, you can apply AR coatings using sol-gel dip coating (see previous lesson) or buy pre-coated glass. For a mirror coating, you deposit a reflective metal (silver or aluminum) on glass. Traditional mirror making uses silver nitrate and a reducing sugar (Tollens' reaction). In a small workshop: clean glass, sensitize with stannous chloride, then spray a mixture of silver nitrate and glucose. The silver deposits as a thin film. Then protect with copper and paint. This is hazardousâuse gloves, goggles, and ventilation. Silver nitrate costs about $50 per 100g. A simpler method: use aluminum mirror coating via vacuum deposition, but that requires a vacuum chamber. For AR coating, you can also use a commercial spray like 'anti-reflective spray' but it's not durable. The best DIY AR is sol-gel silica. For mirrors, you can also buy mirror backing paint and silvering kits from suppliers. In Africa, mirror manufacturing is a viable business: you can cut and frame mirrors. For AR glass, source from suppliers like Pilkington or Chinese manufacturers. Cost of AR glass: $50-$150 per square meter. Applications: solar panel covers, shop windows, and art framing. To test AR quality: use a light meter to compare transmission. For mirrors, check reflectivity with a spectrophotometer or visually. Safety: silver nitrate stains skin and is toxic. Store in dark bottles. Dispose of waste properly. For a small business, focus on cutting and installing AR glass and mirrors. You can also offer 'museum glass' which is AR and UV-filtering. Learn to identify quality: AR glass has a slight blue or green tint. Handle by edges. Clean with ammonia-free cleaner. Videos: search 'how to make mirror silvering' and 'anti-reflective coating glass'. This niche can be profitable in African cities with growing construction.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Surface Treatments and Coatings for Glass Processors

Surface treatment is where raw float glass becomes a product with a price premium. A plain 4 mm sheet in Lagos or Nairobi trades as a commodity; the same sheet acid-etched, sandblasted to a pattern, or coated with a low-emissivity (low-E) layer can sell at two to five times the base value. For African processors, the strategic question is not whether to coat, but which treatment matches local demand, energy costs, and import realities.

This practical reference consolidates the six treatment families covered in this module into decision-ready guidance: process parameters, cost drivers, quality checks, and the African market context for each. Use it as a shop-floor aid and as a business planning tool.

Process Comparison: Parameters and Cost Drivers

The table below summarises the six treatment families. Capital and operating figures are indicative for a small-to-medium African processor (5,000â20,000 mÂ²/month capacity) and should be validated with local suppliers.

Table 1 â Surface Treatment Process Comparison for African Glass Processors
Process Key Parameters Capex (USD, indicative) OpEx Driver Typical End-Use
Acid etching / frosting HF/HâSOâ mix, 10â30 s immersion, 20â30 Â°C 15,000â40,000 Acid cost, effluent neutralisation, PPE Privacy glass, shower screens, retail interiors
Sandblasting / abrasive etching Alumina or silica grit 80â220 mesh, 2â6 bar 8,000â25,000 Grit consumption, compressor power, stencil labour Signage, decorative panels, safety glass marking
Chemical Vapour Deposition (CVD) On-line float, 600â650 Â°C, SnClâ precursors Not viable offline Integrated with float line Hard-coated low-E, pyrolytic coatings
Magnetron sputtering (low-E) Vacuum 10â»Â³â10â»âµ Torr, Ag/ZnO targets, 2â6 kW 250,000â900,000 Vacuum pumps, target replacement, argon Architectural low-E, solar control
Sol-gel coatings Dip/roll coat, 100â200 nm, cure 200â400 Â°C 40,000â120,000 Precursor chemicals, curing energy Anti-reflective (PV), self-cleaning
Anti-reflective / mirror Multi-layer AR or Ag/Cu mirror backing 60,000â200,000 Silver, copper, lacquer, cleanroom Solar PV, shopfront mirrors, optical

Sources: Adapted from Glass Processing Technology (Glassman Europe, 2022); Pilkington "Low Emissivity Glass" technical note (2023); and industry capex ranges reported by African glass processors (Rise AFRICA field data, 2023).

African Market Context: Where the Margins Are

Three realities shape coating economics in Africa:

1. Energy cost dominates low-E economics. Magnetron sputtering is power-hungry â a mid-size line draws 200â400 kW continuously. In Nigeria or South Africa, where industrial tariffs can exceed USD 0.12/kWh, energy alone can add USD 3â6/mÂ² to coated glass. This is why most low-E glass sold in Africa is imported coated (from Turkey, China, or the EU) rather than coated locally. Local sputtering only makes sense at high volume or where import duties and freight create a 25â40% landed-cost premium.

2. Wet processes win on capital efficiency. Acid etching and sandblasting have low capex, fast payback, and strong demand from hospitality, retail, and residential privacy segments â markets growing across Nairobi, Accra, Lagos, and Kigali. A sandblasting booth can be profitable at 1,500 mÂ²/month.

3. Sol-gel is the emerging opportunity. Anti-reflective sol-gel coatings for solar PV glass are increasingly relevant as Africa's solar capacity expands (IRENA, 2023). A roll-coat sol-gel line is capital-light compared to sputtering and can serve regional PV assembly plants.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Acid Etching and Abrasive Processes

Hydrofluoric acid (HF) is one of the most dangerous chemicals in glass processing. It penetrates skin and attacks bone and nerve tissue; a splash covering 2â3% of body surface can be fatal if untreated. Mandatory controls: calcium gluconate gel within 30 seconds of exposure, full face shield, acid-resistant apron, nitrile gloves (not latex), and immediate eye-wash stations within 10 metres of the etch bay. Never store HF in glass containers. Sandblasting silica dust causes silicosis â use alumina grit where possible and enforce N95 or supplied-air respirators. Ensure effluent neutralisation to pH 6â9 before discharge; many African municipalities now enforce this under national environmental regulations (e.g., NESREA in Nigeria, NEMA in Kenya).

Quality Control Benchmarks

Buyers of treated glass â architects, PV assemblers, automotive suppliers â specify measurable performance. The table below gives the acceptance criteria you should be able to test or certify.

Table 2 â Quality Acceptance Criteria by Treatment Type
Treatment Key Metric Typical Specification Test Method
Acid etch / frosting Haze / gloss level Haze 30â80%; gloss < 20 GU Haze meter, gloss meter (ASTM D1003)
Sandblasting Surface roughness (Ra) Ra 1â5 Âµm; uniform pattern depth Profilometer, visual standard panel
CVD (pyrolytic) Emissivity, hardness Îµ â¤ 0.20; pencil hardness â¥ 6H Emissometer, ASTM D3363
Magnetron sputtered low-E Emissivity, U-value, Tvis Îµ â¤ 0.05; U â¤ 1.6 W/mÂ²K; Tvis 60â75% Emissometer, spectrophotometer (EN 673)
Sol-gel AR Transmittance gain +2.5 to +4% absolute Tvis UV-Vis spectrophotometer (ASTM E424)
Mirror / AR mirror Reflectance, adhesion R â¥ 85%; no peel after tape test Reflectometer, ASTM D3359 cross-hatch

Sources: ASTM International standards D1003, D3363, D3359, E424; EN 673 (thermal transmittance); and manufacturer data sheets from Pilkington, Saint-Gobain, and Guardian Glass (2023).

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Match process to market first. Confirm local demand (privacy, solar, architectural) before buying equipment â don't buy a sputter line for a market that imports coated glass cheaper.
  2. Verify chemical supply chains. HF, silver targets, and sol-gel precursors are imported in most African markets; secure at least two suppliers and check import lead times.
  3. Budget for effluent and safety infrastructure. Neutralisation tanks, fume extraction, and PPE typically add 15â25% to wet-process capex.
  4. Test every batch. Keep a haze meter, gloss meter, and emissometer on site â buyer disputes are won or lost on documented QC.
  5. Train on HF response annually. Calcium gluconate gel must be in date and within reach; run a drill every quarter.
  6. Consider toll processing. If capex is prohibitive, partner with an existing coater (e.g., in South Africa or Egypt) and focus on cutting, tempering, and distribution.
  7. Document energy cost per mÂ². For sputtering and CVD-adjacent processes, energy is the swing factor in profitability â meter it separately.
  8. Align with standards early. Specify EN 673, ASTM, or SANS (South African) compliance in your sales contracts to avoid rework.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • ASTM International â Standards & Standardization News (free access to standard summaries for glass testing).
  • IRENA â Renewable Energy Statistics and Solar PV Reports (context for AR-coated PV glass demand in Africa).
  • NEMA Kenya â Environmental Management Authority (effluent and chemical handling regulations).
  • NESREA Nigeria â National Environmental Standards and Regulations Enforcement Agency (industrial discharge and hazardous waste rules).
  • National Glass Association (NGA) â Technical Resources (free technical bulletins on coating and fabrication).

Prepared for Rise AFRICA Skills â Glass Processing Module: Surface Treatments and Coatings. Figures are indicative and must be validated against local supplier quotations and regulatory requirements.

quiz.q: What is the main active chemical in acid etching paste for glass?
quiz.explanation: Ammonium bifluoride is commonly used in paste form for safer etching than hydrofluoric acid.

quiz.q: Why is hydrofluoric acid particularly dangerous?
options: A) It causes immediate burns only
B) It penetrates skin and attacks bones
quiz.explanation: HF penetrates skin and can cause systemic toxicity by attacking calcium in bones.

quiz.q: What is a safe neutralizer for acid etching waste?
quiz.explanation: Baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) neutralizes acids safely.

quiz.q: What abrasive should NOT be used for sandblasting due to silicosis risk?
quiz.explanation: Silica sand contains crystalline silica, which causes silicosis when inhaled.

quiz.q: What is the recommended pressure range for sandblasting glass?
quiz.explanation: 60-90 PSI is typical for glass sandblasting to avoid cracking.

quiz.q: What type of respirator is needed for sandblasting?
quiz.explanation: A P100 respirator filters fine abrasive particles effectively.

quiz.q: What is the typical thickness of a CVD low-E coating?
quiz.explanation: CVD low-E coatings are typically 10-50 nm thick.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of CVD low-E glass?
options: A) It can be tempered after coating
B) It is cheaper than sputtered
quiz.explanation: CVD (pyrolytic) low-E is durable and can be tempered.

quiz.q: At what temperature does online CVD typically occur?
quiz.explanation: Online CVD is done at around 600Â°C on the float glass line.

quiz.q: What is the function of the silver layer in low-E coatings?
quiz.explanation: Silver reflects infrared radiation, reducing heat transfer.

quiz.q: Why must sputtered low-E glass be edge-deleted before making IGUs?
quiz.explanation: The soft coating prevents sealants from bonding, so it must be removed at edges.

quiz.q: What is the typical emissivity of a good low-E coating?
quiz.explanation: Low-E coatings have low emissivity, typically 0.05-0.15.

quiz.q: Which process is used to make sputtered low-E glass?
quiz.explanation: Magnetron sputtering deposits thin films in a vacuum.

quiz.q: What is a common precursor for sol-gel silica coatings?
quiz.explanation: TEOS is a standard precursor for sol-gel silica.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of baking sol-gel coatings at high temperature?
options: B) To increase density and durability
quiz.explanation: Baking densifies the coating and improves adhesion.

quiz.q: Which sol-gel coating provides self-cleaning properties?
quiz.explanation: Titanium dioxide is photocatalytic and breaks down organic dirt.

quiz.q: What is a simple method to apply sol-gel coatings in a small workshop?
quiz.explanation: Dip coating is low-cost and easy to set up with a pulley system.

quiz.q: What is a common chemical used in traditional mirror silvering?
quiz.explanation: Silver nitrate is reduced to metallic silver in mirror making.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of anti-reflective (AR) coatings?
options: B) Reduce glare and increase transmission
quiz.explanation: AR coatings reduce reflection, allowing more light through.

quiz.q: What safety gear is essential when handling silver nitrate?
quiz.explanation: Silver nitrate is toxic and stains skin, so full protection is needed.

quiz.q: What is the typical cost range for sputtered low-E glass per square meter?
quiz.explanation: Sputtered low-E glass typically costs $40-$100 per square meter.

quiz.q: Which of these is a disadvantage of sol-gel coatings?
quiz.explanation: Sol-gel coatings scratch easily unless properly baked.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a stannous chloride sensitizer in mirror making?
quiz.explanation: Stannous chloride helps silver deposit evenly on glass.

quiz.q: Which type of low-E glass is more durable and can be tempered?
quiz.explanation: CVD low-E is pyrolytic and can withstand tempering.

quiz.q: What is the approximate cost of aluminum oxide abrasive per kg in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Aluminum oxide typically costs $2-$5 per kg.

quiz.q: What is a common application of acid-etched glass?
quiz.explanation: Acid etching creates frosted privacy glass.

quiz.q: What is the role of a resist in sandblasting?
options: B) Mask areas to remain clear
quiz.explanation: Resist masks areas that should not be etched.

quiz.q: Which gas is commonly used in sputtering to eject target atoms?
quiz.explanation: Argon ions bombard the target in magnetron sputtering.

quiz.q: What is a simple test for sol-gel coating adhesion?
quiz.explanation: The tape test checks if coating adheres or peels off.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of using CVD low-E glass in African buildings?
options: A) It is cheaper than clear glass
C) It is easier to cut
quiz.explanation: Low-E glass reduces heat gain, lowering air conditioning costs.
